name: National mysticism
summary: National mysticism treats the nation as a spiritually meaningful community with an enduring identity or transcendent mission. Scholarship uses the description across different national and religious settings; the common conception of nationhood leaves most detailed political institutions and policies unspecified.
scope: The broad descriptive family of nationalisms assigning spiritual significance to the national community: Cocău discusses organic national unity and a mystical national soul; Costea Dorle explicitly identifies national mysticism in Vasile Marin’s spiritual nationalism; Lutz identifies it in Gamsakhurdia’s cosmic account of national mission (s5–s7). These sources do not define the family as the combined programmes of Fichte, the Völkisch movement and the Romanian Legion, as the earlier Wikipedia-led scope did. Particular thinkers and movements establish association and illustrate the category, but their unrelated policies are not inherited as family tenets. No specific state or ruling-party doctrine is the record of this family as a whole. Söderman’s Swedish case (s8, pp. 307–308) likewise names national mysticism through an inherited national soul; its monarchism does not define the whole family.
